— Mikel Rosenthal · product design method

Ten steps from a brief to something a team can build.

This is what I say when someone asks to see how I work. Every step names what I decide, who I'm talking to, and which skill file fires and why. The worked example is a pet-care app I built in four hours for an interview exercise, and all of it is public.

Arrow keys to move N · speaker notes I · jump to any slide Cmd‑P · print with notes
Open with this

"I'm going to walk you through how I actually work, front to back. Ten steps, and I'll be specific at every one: what I decide, who I'm talking to, and where I hand work off to the machine. But I want to start with three things that actually happened, because those are the ones you'll remember."

— Before you start talking

For you, not for them. Read it, then close it.

  1. 01Say the number first. "Step three is the setup." People can follow a numbered thing. They can't follow a stream.
  2. 02If you lose the thread, go to a story. Say "let me give you a specific one," then describe what was on the screen. Describing a place restarts your speech when the abstract answer has gone. That is what the next slide is for.
  3. 03Finish each step with the thing it produced. "And what comes out of that is the not‑building table." The output is what makes it real to somebody listening.

Three stories beat twenty bullets. A story you lived is one thing to remember. Bullets are twenty, and twenty is what fails you in the room.

Four parts, and what to cut when the clock moves

Part IFrame · stance, credentials, the ledger. Never cut the credentials slide.
Part IIThe ten steps · the spine, with four evidence slides interleaved.
Part IIIRunning it for real · scope and money, client data, constraints, no‑PRD, handing it on. This is the part hiring managers ask about.
Part IVAppendix · the shelf, the scripts, the failures, the live‑run offer.

Three lengths

2 minSteps 2, 3, 8, 10 and the prototype slide.
10 minPart I, all ten steps at one sentence each, then let them pick two.
40 minParts I to III in order. Appendix only if asked.

When you lose your place

Go back to the spine: read → frame → rig → risk → align → define → direct → build → test → hand off. Ten verbs. Say the verb, then say the artifact.

For you

Don't show this one. It's for you, five minutes before the call. The only thing that matters on it: if you lose the thread, don't reach for the next bullet. Say "let me give you a specific one" and start describing what was on the screen. That always restarts.

— Part I · before any of the process

Three things that actually happened. Everything after this comes out of them.

One · the word that wasn't there

On the screen: a set of user stories for a pet‑care app. All of them consistent with each other. Nothing flagged, nothing obviously missing.

What I noticed: you could schedule care and you could watch a pet, but there was nowhere for anyone to say a thing was done.

What I did: raised it in the first week instead of quietly designing it in, and made "would the watcher feel checked up on" the first thing we tested.

What it taught me: a model won't find an absence, because nothing in the document says it's missing. That part is still my job.

Two · the red that had to go

On the screen: the first pass at an overdue task. Red dot, red text, the word OVERDUE in a red pill. Textbook, and produced in about four seconds.

What I noticed: the person being flagged is a volunteer feeding somebody else's cat. Red shouts at a person doing you a favour.

What I did: amber, and it surfaces by moving up the list rather than by shouting. There is no red anywhere in the shipped token file.

What it taught me: it hands you the most likely design, confidently. The most likely design is nobody's in particular.

Three · five blues

On the screen: a sales tool at Avant, 2021. Three years of separate teams shipping into the same product. No AI anywhere near this one.

What I noticed: I counted every production surface before drawing anything. Five different primary blues. Three button shapes. Three type stacks.

What I did: put the count in front of the people who fund things.

What it taught me: "this is inconsistent" gets you nowhere. "Advisors close six‑figure deals in here, and inconsistency reads as unreliability" gets the work funded.

Say this

"Before I get into how I work, three things that actually happened, because these are the ones you'll remember and I'll keep coming back to them. One, I found a word missing from a spec everyone had already signed off on. Two, the machine handed me a confident answer that was wrong for the product, and the job was knowing why. Three, back in 2021, before any of this tooling existed, I counted five different blues in a live product, and that count is what got the rebuild paid for." · Note to self: each of these needs a room and a person in it when you say it out loud. That part is yours, not on the slide.

— The whole thing on one screen

Ten steps. Six are mine, three are shared, one is mostly the machine.

Human‑led, AI barely present Paired, decision stays with me AI carries the volume, I curate
Say this

"Ten steps. The colour tells you who's driving. The middle is where the machine does real volume, drafting and building. Both ends are almost entirely me, and that's not modesty. That's the part that's hard to replace."

Say this

"If you'd rather I used double diamond language, or whatever your team calls it, this is the same thing in your words. The one row that doesn't translate is step three, setting up the AI. That step is genuinely new. Everything else is the process you already run, done faster."

— Before the steps, the posture

If the team already has product people, the worst thing I can do is try to be one.

It isn't my job to decide what the business should do. It's to make the choices visible, build the thing that answers the question, and make sure what ships is what we agreed on. So I hold three things:

  1. iThe problem's shape. Kept honest, kept in front of everyone, revised in public.
  2. iiThe artifact that resolves arguments. A prototype beats an opinion, every time.
  3. iiiThe gap between intent and build. I'm the person who notices at 80% that the empty state was never designed.

What this buys the room

Holding those three means I'm not competing with anyone over scope. I'm taking out the two things that cost the most on any project: a team that quietly disagrees about the problem, and a build that drifts away from the design.

The most useful decision on any project is usually what we are not building.
Say this

"One thing before the steps. If a team already has product people and a TPM, the worst thing I can do is try to be one of them. So I hold three things instead. The shape of the problem, the artifact that settles arguments, and the gap between what we agreed and what's actually on staging. Everything after this is in service of one of those three."

— Part I · the method did not arrive last year

Twenty-odd years of shipping, most of it where being wrong is expensive.

Where the constraints were real

GE Healthcare, Blue Cross Blue Shield, AbbVie, Catamaran. Regulated categories where every asset meets a reviewer before it meets a member, and a design mistake is a compliance event rather than a bad Dribbble day.

Where the craft was judged

Campaign and product work for Nike, Disney, Crate & Barrel, Whirlpool, Herman Miller, Aflac. Identity through interface, not one or the other.

Recognition

Red Dot Award for Interface Design, 2020, for GE Healthcare's Edison system. Fast Company Innovation by Design. dmi:DVA.

The ten steps are not a new enthusiasm. They are twenty years of process with the expensive parts made cheap.

mikelrosenthal.com
Say this

"Quick bit of background, because these slides can read like I discovered design last year. It's twenty-odd years. A lot of it at GE Healthcare, Blue Cross, AbbVie, where everything you make goes past a reviewer before a member ever sees it. Red Dot in 2020 for GE's Edison system. The process isn't new. What's new is that the expensive parts of it got cheap."

— The honest ledger

Where the decisions are mine, and where I'm just buying hours.

Only me

Finding the absence in a spec. Every scope cut. Which research question gets asked first. The decision rule, written before the study. Taste: the amber, not the red. Whether the team should have the argument now or later.

Paired, decision mine

Edge‑case enumeration then curation. Data‑model options then the choice. Copy variants then the tone call. Direction studies then the kill. Acceptance criteria drafted then rewritten with QA.

The machine

Reading everything and synthesizing it. First prose drafts. Front‑end build at production speed. Cross‑reference integrity across five documents. Token and component doc generation. The consistency passes humans are worst at.

Neither of us could have done that alone in an afternoon. That's the whole argument.
Say this

"Here's the honest split. Left column is me, and it's the column where things actually get decided. Right column is volume. But most of the work lives in the middle: the machine gives me options, I pick one, and I'm the one who has to defend the pick. If you take one thing from this deck, take the middle column."

— What the tooling actually buys

Four things this buys me, and speed is the least interesting one.

Time

The exercise is roughly three days of work compressed into four hours. Not because I type faster. Because the archaeology, the first drafts, and the consistency passes stopped costing days.

Components

Tokens, variants, states, and the library get built once and bound both ways. An engineer builds against tokens instead of measuring screenshots.

Terms

A definitions table that is actually maintained. Watcher, routine, occurrence, handoff. Every doc, ticket, and component uses the same word for the same thing, and that stops being an aspiration.

Annotations

The reasoning travels with the artifact. Why amber and not red, why the undo window is five minutes, which state this is. The prototype carries its own spec.

The dividend I care most about is the fourth. Speed is easy to demonstrate and easy to dismiss. Annotation is what turns a fast prototype into something an engineer can build from without me in the room.

Say this

"Everyone assumes the win here is speed. Speed is real, but it's the least interesting part. The other three are what change the handoff. The component system gets built properly because it's finally cheap to build properly. The words stay consistent. And the reasoning gets written down while I still remember why I decided it."

01 Intake · day one, first two hours · human‑led

Day one I'm reading, not drawing.

  1. 1.1Read the brief twice with no tools open. Once for what it says, once for what it assumes. This is the only step where using AI would actively cost me something, because the first read is where absences are noticeable and a summary smooths them away.
  2. 1.2Inventory everything that exists. The PRD, old research, analytics, support tickets, the stakeholder emails nobody rereads, the competitor set, any existing design file. Ask for it explicitly and in writing.
  3. 1.3Put all of it in one repo. Documents in, one folder, versioned. This is what makes the machine useful at step three, and it is also just good practice.
  4. 1.4Ask for a synthesis and a contradiction list. Not a summary. Specifically: where do these documents disagree with each other, and what does each one assume without stating?
  5. 1.5Send five questions, in writing, same day. Written questions get written answers, and written answers become the decision log.
Who I'm talking to
PM · asking for materials Strategist · what was decided before me Support or CS · the complaints
Skill files
full-output-enforcementBans truncation and placeholder patterns. An inventory that ends in "and 14 others" is a useless inventory.
design:research-synthesisStructures prior research into themes and open questions instead of a flat recap.
every taste and imagegen skillDeliberately off. Nothing is being designed yet, and loading a visual skill here biases the read.
Say this

"Day one I'm not designing anything, I'm reading. Everything goes into one place: the brief, the old research, the tickets, the stakeholder emails nobody's opened in a year. The machine reads all of it, which used to eat my first week. But the part I won't give up is reading the brief twice myself first, cold, with nothing else open. That's the only time I'll catch what's missing. Once I've read a summary it's gone."

02 Assessment · the same day · human‑led

My first job is finding what the document doesn't say.

Asked to "review these user stories," a model produces auth flows and CRUD refinements, because absences do not pattern‑match. Finding the hole is still the designer's job. These are the seven probes I run, in order, by hand.

1 · The absence test

What does this product not let anyone do? Not a missing feature, a missing category.

2 · The ending test

What happens when it works? Every flow has a finish. Find the one nobody designed.

3 · The second‑user test

The doc is written for one user. Who else touches this, and what do they see?

4 · The lifecycle test

Invited, active, expired, revoked, returned. Which of those states does the spec actually cover?

5 · The three unloved states

Empty, first run, failure. Nobody writes user stories for them and every product has them.

6 · The cost test

Which sentence in this PRD is a schema decision wearing a UX costume?

7 · The counter‑metric test

What number would tell us we are fooling ourselves? If it isn't instrumented, we will never ask.

Then: what do I do with it?

Not design it quietly. Raise it in week zero, in the room, with the strategist present.

PetWatch, what the probes found
probe 2 · the ending testThe user stories describe a product with no completion state. You can schedule care and you can watch a pet, but nothing in the stories lets anyone say "done." That is a category error, not a missing feature.
probe 3 · the second userEverything was written for the owner. The watcher, the person doing the actual favor, was the one with no product.
probe 6 · the cost test"Recurring routines" is a data‑model decision. Materialize occurrences and you buy a cron job, a backfill horizon, and a migration every edit.
Skill files
none, on purposeThis step is a person reading closely. The machine comes back in at step three, once I know what I think.
Say this

"This is the step I'd want you to judge me on. I run the same seven questions at any spec. The one that found the pet app was number two: what happens when it works? Nothing did. You could schedule care, you could watch a pet, but there was nowhere to say a thing was done. And the stories were all consistent with each other, which is exactly why it's hard to see, and why a model won't catch it. Nothing in the document says it's missing."

03 The rig · twenty minutes, once · paired

What actually happens when I "put the PRD into Claude."

  1. 3.1A repo, not a chat. /artifacts for the docs, /prototype for the build, /assets, one build script. Chats are disposable, repos are reviewable, and a client can be handed a repo.
  2. 3.2A CLAUDE.md that encodes the constraints. Product vocabulary, the non‑goals, the tone rules, accessibility floor, the stack the client's team actually uses. This is the project's design brief written for a machine, and I write it by hand.
  3. 3.3Choose the skill files. Deliberately, and out loud. Loading the wrong one is worse than loading none, because a strong aesthetic skill will confidently drag a product UI toward a landing page.
  4. 3.4Set the three dials. Variance, motion, density. These are numbers, not vibes, and they get set from the brief rather than from my mood.
  5. 3.5Make it state the design read back to me. One line, before anything is generated. If the read is wrong, I found out in ten seconds instead of after a build.
  6. 3.6Name the artifacts up front. PRD, backlog, research plan, ways of working, AI log, prototype. Named before drafted, so scope creep is visible.
The dials, PetWatch setting
DESIGN_VARIANCE4
MOTION_INTENSITY3
VISUAL_DENSITY5

The library baseline is 8 / 6 / 4, tuned for landing pages. PetWatch is a care‑coordination tool used by an anxious volunteer at 7am. Variance down, motion down, density up. Setting these is a design decision, and I say so.

The design read, verbatim

"Reading this as: multi‑user care‑coordination product for anxious non‑technical watchers, with a calm utility language, leaning toward a hand‑built token set and no motion beyond state feedback."

Say this

"When I say I put the brief into Claude, this is what I actually mean, and it's more deliberate than it sounds. It goes in a repo, not a chat window. I hand-write a constraints file: the vocabulary, what we're not building, the accessibility floor. Then I choose which of my skill files load. And I set three dials. For this one I turned variance and motion down and density up, because it's a tool somebody uses at seven in the morning, one-handed, while a cat yells at them. It is not a landing page."

04 Risk and research · week one · paired

I don't research everything. I research what would collapse the product if I'm wrong about it.

  1. 4.1List the assumptions and rank them by cost of being wrong. Not by how curious I am. A1 is the one that kills the product.
  2. 4.2Write the decision rule before the study runs. "Four of six watchers react neutrally or better, we build the active version. Three or more find it accusatory, we ship passive." Pre‑committed, so I can't rationalize afterwards.
  3. 4.3Pick the cheapest method that can falsify it. Six interviews beats a hundred survey responses when the question is about feeling watched.
  4. 4.4I run the interviews myself. You don't delegate listening. The thing you're listening for is the pause before the answer.
  5. 4.5Synthesis the same afternoon, then I argue with it. I check every theme against a quote and throw out the ones that are just the model agreeing with my hypothesis.

A research plan without a pre‑committed decision rule is a plan to be persuaded by whatever you find.

Who I'm talking to
Strategist · agreeing what A1 is PM · recruiting and scheduling Six real users · me, alone, listening
Skill files
design:user-researchDrafts the screener and the discussion guide from the assumption, then I cut the leading questions it always writes.
design:research-synthesisClusters transcripts into themes with quote evidence, same day rather than same week.
PetWatch, A1

"Does a watcher experience task completion as accountability or as surveillance?" Having found the gap, the reflexive move is to design it. Stopping to ask whether the watcher would hate it is the product judgment.

Say this

"I don't research everything. I rank the assumptions by what it costs me to be wrong, and I write the decision rule before the study runs so I can't talk myself into whatever I find. On the pet app the risky one wasn't whether people want a checklist. It was whether the person doing you a favour ends up feeling checked up on. The machine writes the guide and does the synthesis the same afternoon. I do the interviews myself. You don't hand off listening."

05 Alignment · week zero, 90 minutes · human‑led

Ninety minutes, everyone in the room, and I'm running it rather than presenting to it.

  1. 5.1Problem framing, out loud. Everyone writes the problem in one sentence, silently, then we read them. They always disagree, and it's much cheaper to find that out in a room than in cycle four.
  2. 5.2One number. We leave agreeing on a single measure of whether this worked. I bring a proposal, but the point is that we pick one, not that mine wins.
  3. 5.3The v1 cut line. Not a roadmap, a line. What is not in v1, written down, with the trigger that would change it.
  4. 5.4The riskiest assumption, named, owned, scheduled.
  5. 5.5This is where I raise the gap. In week zero, in a room, with the strategist present. Not in a document three weeks later, and not by quietly designing it in and hoping nobody notices. The stories came from someone. They deserve the argument face to face.

Much cheaper to find that out now than in week nine. We leave with one metric, a line for what's not in v1, and one page that becomes the truth. And this is where I raise the gap I found earlier. 06 Definition · week one to two · AI carries volume

I make the decisions, it writes the first draft, and I rewrite until it sounds like me.

  1. 6.1Outline by hand, dictate the decisions. Every section heading and every call is mine before a word of prose exists.
  2. 6.2The definitions table first. Watcher, routine, occurrence, handoff, completion. One word per concept, fixed early, and then every document, ticket, and component name obeys it. This is the cheapest quality intervention on any project.
  3. 6.3The not‑building table. The part of any PRD I'm proudest of. Models are additive by disposition, they always want to add, so deciding what not to build is where the design actually happens.
  4. 6.4Flows, screen inventory, states, data model, with the data model written as a question for the backend engineer rather than a decree.
  5. 6.5Backlog with acceptance criteria and analytics events on the same ticket. A separate instrumentation ticket is a ticket that does not get built.
  6. 6.6The consistency pass. Every ID, ticket number and cross‑reference aligned across five documents. The thing humans are worst at and machines are perfect at, running on every save.
Skill files

anthropic-skills:docx · pptxWhen the client lives in Word and slides rather than Notion. Meet them where they read.
The correction I always make

Drafted copy slides toward compliance language: "verify," "confirm," "task overdue." Individually fine. In aggregate they build the surveillance product the research plan is worried about. Tone gets enforced line by line, and it drifts back.

all five artifacts
Say this

"I outline it and talk through the decisions, the machine writes the first draft, and then I rewrite until it sounds like me. Two things I'd point at. The definitions table, fixed early, so every document and ticket and component uses the same word for the same thing. And the not-building table, which is my favourite part of any spec, because these models will add forever, and deciding what to leave out is where the design actually happens."

07 Direction · a day, not a week · paired

Three directions with a reason each, then I kill two in front of people.

  1. 7.1Write the direction as a sentence before it's a picture. "Calm utility that never shouts at a volunteer." If the sentence is weak, the comps will be decorative.
  2. 7.2Generate three, not one. Each pinned to a different reading of the audience. One image per screen or section, never a compressed board, because a compressed board hides the decisions.
  3. 7.3Kill two out loud, with the reason. The kill is the deliverable. Showing three and asking "which do you like" hands the decision to whoever speaks first.
  4. 7.4Tokens, not screenshots. The surviving direction becomes a token file the same day. Color, type scale, spacing, radius, state colors.
  5. 7.5Check the direction against the constraint, not the taste. Contrast in both themes, target sizes, the 7am one‑handed case.
Skill files
imagegen-frontend-web · imagegen-frontend-mobileOne image per section or screen, forced composition variety so the three directions are genuinely different rather than three palettes of the same layout.
minimalist-uiThe direction that won on PetWatch. Warm monochrome, typographic contrast, flat surfaces, no gradients.
industrial-brutalist-uiGenerated as direction two. Right for an ops dashboard, wrong for a nervous pet owner. Killed with the reason stated.

The taste call, PetWatch

First pass at overdue styling came back red and urgent. Standard pattern, confidently produced, wrong product. It shouts at a volunteer doing you a favor. Amber, surfaced by position rather than alarm, and the reasoning is a note on the prototype.

08 The artifact · the stage AI changed most · AI carries volume

The prototype used to come last. Now it comes early, and it's what ends arguments.

  1. 8.1The state model is mine, and it comes first. What states exist, what transitions are legal, what is optimistic and what is confirmed. This is the design work. Everything after it is execution.
  2. 8.2Interaction decisions before build. Optimistic completion with a five‑minute undo. A sheet system rather than page transitions. Written down, then built.
  3. 8.3Build tokens, then components, then screens. In that order, so the third screen costs a tenth of the first.
  4. 8.4Every state gets built, including the ugly ones. Empty, loading, error, offline, expired invite, two watchers colliding. Cheap now, so there's no excuse.
  5. 8.5Annotate as I go, not after. Design notes live on the prototype: what this state is, why this choice, what it costs. The reasoning is worth more than the pixels and it evaporates within a week.
  6. 8.6Click it myself, on a phone, at the real size. Then fix what's wrong with the thumb reach.

I make the state model and the interaction calls. The machine builds the front end. Every state gets built, including empty and error and offline, because there's no excuse not to any more. And I write the notes as I go, while I still know why I did it."

08 Evidence · the artifact itself, annotations included

Say this

"So this is the thing itself. On the left there's a clock you can move, so you're not taking my word for what happens at 7:15 when the insulin is late. The middle is the running product. And that rail on the right is ten design notes tied to the screen. Honestly, that rail is the handoff. It's the reasoning travelling with the artifact instead of disappearing the week after I leave. It's live at that address right now if you want to poke at it."

09 Pressure test · ongoing · paired

Edge cases are the one place the machine is actually better than me.

  1. 9.1Run the edge‑case sweep, then curate it by hand. Invite states, timezone traps, revocation while the app is open. "What happens if the invite link is opened while logged into the wrong account" is what a tired human misses at 4pm and QA finds in week six.
  2. 9.2Turn the survivors into test cases at refinement, not bugs at QA. The list exists so QA is not the first person to think about the expired invite.
  3. 9.3Accessibility pass against the build, not the mockup. Contrast in both themes, target size, focus order, the screen‑reader path through the completion flow.
  4. 9.4Critique my own work with the constraints loaded. Adversarial, against the brief, before anyone else sees it.
  5. 9.5Wednesday desk check on staging, 30 minutes, with QA and eng. The ritual I'd fight to keep. Figma tells you what was intended. Staging tells you what exists. The gap between them is where products quietly get worse.
  6. 9.6Seeded staging fixtures from cycle one. A pet with a full week of tasks, a pending invite, an expired invite, a revoked watcher. Otherwise every review happens against an empty database and we ship a product that has only been seen at its best.
Who I'm working with
QA · co‑writing acceptance criteria Eng · desk check on staging DevOps · the seeded fixtures
Skill files
design:accessibility-reviewContrast, focus order, target size, semantics, checked against the built thing.
design:design-critiqueStructured critique with the brief loaded, so the feedback is against intent rather than preference.
code-review · security-reviewOn the prototype code, because a prototype an engineer will read should not teach them bad patterns.
The one ticket with a dedicated pass

The double‑completion guard. The safety label is not decoration. It is the ticket where failure means an animal gets fed twice or not at all.

Say this

"Edge cases are the one place the machine is genuinely better than me, not just quicker. What happens if someone opens the invite link while logged into the wrong account is exactly the thing I miss at four in the afternoon and QA finds in week six. So I generate the list early and then go through it by hand. And mid-cycle we look at staging, not mockups. Figma tells you what we meant. Staging tells you what exists."

10 Handoff · and after · human‑led

A handoff works if they stop needing me in the room.

  1. 10.1The decision log. What we chose, what we rejected, and what would reopen each call. The last column is the one nobody writes and the one everybody needs in month four.
  2. 10.2The annotated prototype as the interaction spec. Static redlines cannot describe optimistic completion with a five‑minute undo. A clickable artifact can.
  3. 10.3Tokens in a format a pipeline eats. Standard DTCG that Style Dictionary consumes, not a screenshot of a palette.
  4. 10.4Docs generated from the same source as the components, so they physically cannot drift. Component metadata carries a checksum: edit a component without updating docs and the build reports them stale and exits non‑zero.
  5. 10.5Code Connect, so Figma components and React components are bound. Handoff stops being a throw over a wall and becomes a link between two representations of one component.
  6. 10.6A skill file for their team. The system's rules, written so their own AI tooling inherits them on day one. Optional, never a dependency.
  7. 10.7After launch, I bring the counter‑metric back. Week one, with evidence rather than instinct. Instrumented before launch, because it's the number nobody asks for later.
Skill files
design:design-handoffAssembles the package and catches what's missing from it.
figma:figma-code-connectBinds Figma components to their React counterparts. When a token changes, both sides know.
figma:figma-generate-libraryThe published library the engineers actually build against.
anthropic-skills:skill-creatorWrites the client‑facing skill file, so the rules survive me leaving.
stitch-design-tasteThe DESIGN.md that lets their team generate new screens that still look like the product.
Nothing here requires AI

Generated docs, standard tokens, a decision log, an annotated prototype. The skill file is a bonus for whenever the team is ready, not a condition of the handoff working.

Say this

"Handoff is a package, not a goodbye deck. Decision log, and every row says what would make us reopen it. The annotated prototype as the spec for how it behaves. Tokens in a format your build actually eats. Docs generated from the same source as the components so the two can't drift apart. And a skill file, so if your team uses this tooling they inherit the rules on day one. The test I hold myself to is whether they still need me in the room, and they shouldn't."

10 Evidence · what engineering actually receives

Say this

"And this is what engineering gets. Three tiers. Raw values, then what a colour is for, then where it lands in the UI. Engineers never touch a hex code. Re-theme the bottom layer and nothing above it changes, which is how this survived a whole major version. Those links are live."

— Part III · running it for real

What the ten steps look like inside a six-week build.

WeekSteps liveWhat the client sees on Friday
001 02 03The gap, named, and five written questions. The workshop is booked.
104 05One metric, a v1 cut line, the riskiest assumption owned. Research in the field.
206 07Draft PRD with the not‑building table. Three directions, two killed out loud.
308A clickable prototype. Not a deck about one.
408 09Every state built, including empty and error. Edge cases become test cases.
509 10Desk check on staging. Tokens published, components bound.
610Decision log, annotated prototype, generated docs, skill file. I become optional.

The receipt, honestly accounted

Brief, thesis, scoping40m
PRD, backlog, research plan, ways of working1h 20m
Prototype: direction, build, testing, annotation1h 30m
Submission hub, AI log, final read30m

Four hours, five documents and a working prototype. Unassisted that scope is roughly three days, and the honest four‑hour alternative is static frames and a shorter document.

Where the compression is real, and where it is not

Compresses hard: archaeology, first drafts, the build, consistency passes, edge‑case enumeration, doc generation.
Refuses to compress: the workshop, the interviews, the scope argument, review cycles, and every hour that is actually someone else's calendar.

Rates and exact hours are per engagement. What I commit to is the shape, and to telling you at kickoff which weeks are mine and which belong to your review cycle.

Say this

"If you want it in project terms: there's a clickable prototype at the end of week three, not week nine, and week six is me making myself unnecessary. The honest part is on the right. What compresses is drafting, building, consistency. What doesn't compress is the workshop, the interviews, the argument about scope, and your review cycles. I'd rather say that at kickoff than have you find it out in week four."

— Part III · the question every client asks second

What am I actually putting into it, and who signed off?

  1. iIt runs in a repo I control, not a chat window. On the PetWatch exercise the entire toolchain was Claude Code and a browser. No other AI tools, and that is in the log.
  2. iiWhat goes in: the brief, the materials the client handed me, my own outlines and decisions. That is the working set.
  3. iiiWhat never goes in without written sign‑off: PHI or PII, production credentials, unreleased financials, and anything under a third‑party NDA that is not mine to put there.
  4. ivVendor posture gets confirmed per engagement, in writing, before the first upload. Retention, whether inputs train anything, and indemnification for generated assets. Discovered in legal is too late.
  5. vEvery generated asset passes a human review gate before it reaches a client, a member, or a patient. The gate is a person, and it is named.
  6. viThe AI usage log ships with the project, failures included, so nobody has to reconstruct what was machine‑drafted a year later.

Why this is not paperwork in a regulated category

Generative output runs into implied clinical claims, synthetic people who read as patients or clinicians, and model licensing that may or may not carry indemnification. Most teams meet all three late, usually in review, usually with a launch date already public.

Sorting this out up front is what lets a regulated client say yes at all.
Say this

"The second question I always get is what I'm feeding these things, so I answer it before it's asked. It runs in a repo I control, not a chat window. What goes in is the brief, whatever you handed me, and my own decisions. What doesn't go in without written sign-off is patient data, credentials, anything under someone else's NDA. And I get retention and indemnification confirmed in writing before the first upload, not after legal finds it. In healthcare that last one is the whole ballgame."

— Part III · the conditions that break most AI workflows

The same ten steps, under the constraints that actually show up.

No user access, because legal or clinical says no

Research moves to proxies: support tickets, call transcripts, the SMEs who talk to members all day. The decision rule still gets written before the study. Proxy evidence with a pre‑committed rule beats no evidence with a strong opinion.

Legal, medical and brand review in the chain

Reviewers sit in the week‑zero room, not at the end of it. Every generated asset carries provenance. Copy runs the claims check before it runs the taste check, because a beautiful line that implies an outcome is a rewrite either way.

The client bans external AI tools

The method still runs. The dials become a written design brief, the skill files become a principles doc, the prototype gets built by hand and takes longer. I tell you how much longer at kickoff rather than quietly absorbing it.

A legacy product with no system

Audit first, always. Read the current variance, motion and density before proposing new ones, then upgrade without breaking behaviour. The Avant audit two slides back is what that looks like.

The timeline is four weeks, not six

Steps do not get skipped, they get shortened. The one I refuse to cut is the week‑zero alignment, because a team that disagrees about the problem will spend the saved fortnight twice over.

A stakeholder who has already decided

Build the thing that makes the disagreement visible rather than arguing. A prototype turns "I don't like it" into "this state is wrong," which is a conversation you can actually finish.

Say this

"None of this is worth much if it only works on an easy project, so here's the same process under the conditions that actually turn up. The one I'd point at is the third. If you don't want external AI tools anywhere near this, the process still runs. It just costs more, and I'll tell you the number at kickoff instead of quietly eating it."

— Part III · the other entry point

Half the time there's no document at all. Just an idea and a budget.

  1. 0.1Write the PRD they didn't. One page, in their words, back to them inside 48 hours. It is the most useful unpaid hour in any project.
  2. 0.2Run the one‑sentence problem exercise on a call rather than in a workshop. Three people, three sentences, read aloud. The disagreement arrives on day two instead of week five.
  3. 0.3Name three things it is not. Non‑goals are easier to agree on than goals, and they define the shape faster.
  4. 0.4Build the cheapest artifact that makes the disagreement visible. Usually one screen. Sometimes one paragraph of the empty state.
  5. 0.5Then step 02 as normal, run against the document I just wrote. If my own PRD has a hole in it, better I find it than they do.
Writing the spec they never wrote is the fastest way to find out whether they agree with themselves.

And it puts me where I want to be

Whoever writes the problem down ends up holding its shape. That is the first of the three things I said I hold, and on a project with no document it is available to whoever moves first.

What I do not do

Start designing to look responsive. A fast comp against an unwritten problem is the most expensive artifact in this business, because everyone starts reacting to it and nobody goes back to the question.

Say this

"The deck says a spec lands in my inbox, and honestly, half the time that's a lie. Usually it's an idea and a budget. So I write the spec they didn't, one page, in their words, back to them within a couple of days. It's the fastest way to find out whether they agree with themselves. And whoever writes the problem down ends up holding it, which is where I want to be. What I don't do is start making comps to look busy."

— Part III · the part that matters if you are hiring a lead

If I'm the only one who can run it, it's a hobby, not a method.

  1. iThe skill files are files. They live in the repo, get reviewed in a pull request, and get edited by whoever is closest to the work. Nothing about this is locked in my head or my account.
  2. iiA designer's first week: read the constraints file, run step 03 on a small ticket, and get critiqued on the design read and the dial settings rather than on the pixels.
  3. iiiCritique changes shape. I review the design read before I review the output, because wrong dials produce confidently wrong work, and that is fixable in one sentence instead of one week.
  4. ivThe failures get logged, not buried. A team that only shares its wins with this tooling will repeat the red‑overdue mistake in every project.
  5. vWhat I will not do: make the tooling a condition of anyone's employment. The handoff package works without it and the skill file is a bonus for whenever the team is ready.

What I would ask you for

One shared repo. Permission to write the constraints file for the project. Design tickets in the delivery cycle rather than a parallel board. And thirty minutes on a Wednesday to look at staging with an engineer and someone from QA.

That is the whole list. Everything else in this deck I can bring on my own.

I would rather hand over something the team can edit than something they have to ask me about.
Say this

"If you're hiring someone to lead rather than just produce, this is the slide. The skill files are files. They live in the repo, they get reviewed like code, anyone can edit them. When I critique someone working this way, I look at their read and their dial settings before I look at the output, because wrong settings produce confidently wrong work, and that's a one-sentence fix instead of a week. And I won't make any of this a condition of somebody's job."

— Appendix · the human part

Six conversations this process depends on, and how I open each one.

Telling a strategist their spec has a hole

"I read the stories closely and I think there's a category missing rather than a feature. Nothing in them lets anyone finish. I might be wrong about why it's not there, so I'd rather ask than design around it."

Ask what's behind it before proposing. Half the time there's a reason, and knowing it is worth more than being right.

Asking an engineer what's expensive

"Before I commit to this in the design, what does it cost you? If deriving occurrences from rules is harder than materializing them, tell me and I'll solve the same user need a cheaper way."

I've been wrong about this kind of thing before. Say that part out loud.

Writing acceptance criteria with QA

"I want you upstream of me on this one. Here's the edge‑case list from design. Which of these are test cases, and what did I miss?"

"Renders correctly" is not acceptance criteria. Empty, loading, error, offline, and the collision case is.

When a client asks "did AI make this?"

"AI built the front end at production speed from my interaction decisions. The thesis, the scope cuts, and the tone are mine, and I keep a usage log with the failures in it. Ask me about the red overdue styling."

Volunteering the log is what makes the answer credible.

A teammate who doesn't want AI in the loop

"Nothing in the handoff requires it. Generated docs, standard tokens, a decision log. The skill file is there for whenever you want it and the package works without it."

Never make adoption a condition of the work being usable.

Defending a scope cut

"It's in the not‑building table with the trigger that would reopen it. If that trigger fires, I'll bring it back myself."

A cut with a documented reopen condition stops being a refusal and becomes a plan.

Say this

"None of this works without the conversations, so here are the six that carry it. They're all the same shape. Bring the evidence, say out loud what I might be wrong about, and leave the other person a real way to disagree with me."

— Appendix · three receipts

Where the machine was wrong on PetWatch, and why it mattered.

  1. 01Overdue styling came back red and urgent. Standard pattern, confidently produced, wrong product. It shouts at a volunteer doing you a favor. The amber treatment, surfaced by position rather than alarm, is the correction, and the reasoning is now a design note on the prototype itself.
  2. 02The first data‑model draft materialized schedule occurrences into a table. The obvious pattern, and the one that costs a cron job, a backfill horizon, and a migration every time a routine is edited. Deriving occurrences from rules is the simpler system, and choosing it required knowing why the obvious pattern is expensive. The reviewer has to know more than the generator.
  3. 03Drafted copy kept sliding toward compliance language. "Verify," "confirm," "task overdue." Individually fine. In aggregate they build the exact surveillance product the research plan is worried about. Tone had to be enforced line by line, and it drifted back more than once.
It gives you the most likely design. The most likely design is nobody's in particular.

It's confidently generic, which is a harder problem than broken code. What you get is plausible design decisions that nobody actually made.

These three are what I'd show anyone who asks why they still need designers. Making things is cheap now. Knowing which of the things is wrong, and why, is not.

the full AI usage log
Say this

"One honest slide, because a process that only lists wins is an advert. Three places the machine was confidently wrong on this project, and all three mattered. Same pattern every time: it gives you the most likely design, and the most likely design is nobody's in particular. This way of working holds up because there's a person standing exactly where the judgment goes."

— Part IV · the offer

If you would rather see it than hear it, hand me a spec.

Ten minutes, this screen, steps 01 through 03 against a document I have never read. Yours, a competitor's, or something you invent on the call. It is the least rehearsed thing I can offer you, which is exactly why it is worth more than the rest of this deck.

Minute 1 to 3

I read it cold and say what it assumes without stating. No tools open.

Minute 3 to 5

The seven probes, out loud, and the first absence I can defend.

Minute 5 to 8

The rig: constraints file, which skill files load and which stay off, the three dials with reasons.

Minute 8 to 10

The design read, stated back, and the five questions I would send you tonight.

What it will not do

It will not produce a design in ten minutes, and I would be suspicious of anyone who claimed otherwise. It produces the questions I would bring to your Monday, which is the actual first deliverable on every project I have ever run.

If it goes wrong

Then you have watched me be wrong in real time on an unfamiliar document, with my reasoning showing. That is still better information about how I work than a rehearsed slide, and I would rather you had it before you hire me than after.

Say this

"One offer before I stop. If you'd rather see this than hear about it, hand me a spec I've never read, yours or something you make up on the call, and I'll do the first three steps in ten minutes right here. It won't give you a design. It'll give you the questions I'd bring to your Monday. And if it goes badly, you've watched me be wrong in real time with my reasoning showing, which is still better information than a rehearsed slide."

— Land here

Making things got cheap. Deciding what to make didn't. I like this job better than the old one.

Ten steps. The two ends are almost entirely human, the middle is where the machine carries volume, and every one of them has a person's decision in it. The test of the whole thing is step ten: whether the team can keep going without me in the room.
